A shortcoming of the information gain criterion is that it is biased towards splits with larger
k. Given a candidate split, if subdividing any subset provides additional class differentiation,
then the information gain score will always be better. That is, there is no cost to making a
split. In practice, making splits into many small subsets increases the sensitivity to individual
training data items, leading to overfit. If the split’s cardinality k is greater than the number of
class values m, then we might be “overclassifying” the data.
For example, suppose we want to decide whether conditions are suitable for holding a sem-
inar, and one of the attributes is day of the week. The “correct” answer is Monday through
Friday are candidates for a seminar, while Saturday and Sunday are not. This is naturally a
binary split, but ID3 would select a 7-way split.

randomly classified according to the probability distribution of class membership within each
subset. Like ID3, the Gini index is biased towards splits with larger k.

given pointwise semisupervision on some nodes, one can construct semisupervised graph-cut prob-
lems that respects the given information. In particular, the labels may indicate that two nodes with
the same label should remain within the same subgraph after the cut [12, 13]. The same information
can also be conveyed by specifying a must-link relationship between pairs (or subsets) of nodes, so
that the must-linked nodes should ideally belong to the same subgraph. For ease of exposition, we

on such problems in Section 20.6.
Let A 1 be the subset of vertices with cluster id 1, and A 2 be the subset with cluster id 2. Clearly,
A 1 and A 2 are disjoint subsets of V . The semisupervised unnormalized cut problem can be posed
as follows: Find a partitioning (V 1, V 2) such that cut (V 1, V 2) is minimized subject to the constraint
A 1 ⊆ V 1, A 2 ⊆ V 2. In order to achieve balanced cuts, we also consider semisupervised versions of
the ratio-cut (or normalized-cut) problem. In particular, the semisupervised ratio-cut problem can
be posed as follows: Find a partitioning (V 1, V 2) such that Rcut (V 1, V 2) is minimized subject to the
constraint A 1 ⊆ V 1, A 2 ⊆ V 2. Similarly, one can pose the semisupervised normalized-cut problem
using Ncut (V 1, V 2) instead of Rcut (V 1, V 2) above. The problems outlined above are NP-hard, and
there has been some work on developing polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTASs) for
related problems [12, 13].

The previous examples of simulation we discussed did not involve time as an element of the
simulation. Such simulations are referred to as static. However, many systems experience
changes in state over time. For example, inventory and queuing systems have the state vari-

But consider the water behind a dam. Clearly evaporation and heavy rains make the state
variable. The water level experiences changes in state continuously over time. Systems like
this are referred to as continuous simulations.
Consider simulating a network system. For this type of study, the researcher must:
n Identify the system, which is a collection of entities that interact over time to
accomplish the goals of the study.
n Construct a model, or an abstract representation of the system that describes a
system in terms of state, entities and related attributes, sets, events, activities, and
delays.
c The system state is a collection of variables that contain all of the information to
describe the system at any time.
c A set is simply a collection of associated states.
c An event is an occurrence that changes the state of a system.
c A known time interval, such as for servicing an entity, is an activity.
c A time interval of unknown length until an activity is actually completed, such as a
wait time in a queue, is referred to as a delay.

IF
I have buried this a bit under the scads of other functions, but IF is the most important
function of all. It’s a logical function that can evaluate between true and false statements.
The form of the IF statement is simple and contains three parts. The first part is the logi-
cal test itself, which must always return true or false. What are you evaluating? Perhaps
you want to know if the cell is greater than the cell below it. In this case, your logical
test would be something like A2>B2. If the logical test returns true, then the whole IF
function returns the second argument. If it returns false, it returns the third argument.
These arguments can just be text strings like so:
=IF(A2>B2, “Greater”, “Not Greater”)
Thus if A2 is greater than B2, this cell will have the word “Greater” as its data.
Otherwise, it will have “Not Greater” as its data. Until you experiment with this, you
may not realize how powerful this function actually is.
